utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone, both in the courtroom and those outside the courtroom assisting us to perform our functions. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Perhaps just after the recess, we start with the appearances of the parties. Mr. Tieger for the Prosecution, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger and Thomas Hannis on behalf of the Prosecution, assisted by case manager Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence today, I appear with our case manager, Ms. Cmeric, and an intern from the University of Chicago, Mr. Brett Taxin. I would indicate that Mr. Stewart will not be here today. He's attending to other matters at this stage and will be back in court on Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. I then would like do make a few observations at this moment. There are still a couple of outstanding issues which need to be decided. That will follow soon, but not at this very moment. Most of the decisions will be given orally. Then I informed the parties that the Chamber has decided that it wants to receive written statements of witnesses, even if they testify viva voce, in order to be better able to exercise its function of control over the proceedings under Rule 90(F). Then the following matter is that the parties should be aware that even if a witness testifies in closed session or under other protective measures, that it is not always necessary to have the exhibits admitted under seal. Sometimes the exhibits are such do not affect the protective measures at all. Therefore, the parties are invited to check on the list of exhibits that are admitted to see whether there are any exhibits that could be unsealed without affecting the protective measures. This in order to preserve the public character of the proceedings to the highest possible level. Then finally I'd like to invite the parties to ask Madam Registrar to provide them with a list of outstanding exhibits, as you may remember that some exhibits are not decided upon, others, even whole series, we decided to deal with them at one moment. For example, I remember Sanski Most. Madam Registrar has prepared a list of outstanding exhibits. If the parties would go through them so that during one of the following days we could easily identify whether there are any objections or not and what could be admitted and what could not be admitted. The list of Prosecution exhibits is 12 pages and 1 page for Defence exhibits still outstanding. I would leave it to that at this moment as far as procedural matters are concerned, and I would like to ask the Prosecution whether it is ready to call its next witness. As far as I'm aware of, Mr. Tieger, there are no protective measures sought for the next witness. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then your next witness would be Mr. Izet Redzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might indicate that I think there's something that Mr. Krajisnik would like to address the Court in relation to, and on my understanding it's a matter that goes into financial considerations, and of course, all the decisions relating to financial considerations are confidential. So it might be appropriate in those circumstances to deal with that particular issue under closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. But perhaps it would be more practical, since we have now asked the witness to enter the courtroom, to do that today, but at a later moment. Could Mr. Krajisnik indicate how much time he would need to address the Court in respect of this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We did not receive any interpretation. I first thought that I was on the wrong channel, but I'm on channel 4 and do not receive English translation. Yes, the witness may be escorted into the courtroom. And at the same time, I'd like to know what went wrong with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please repeat the information you just gave so that we can see whether we now receive translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take no more than 10 to 15 minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Good afternoon. I take it, Mr. Redzic. Mr. Redzic, before testifying, before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Redzic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, it's you who is going to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll be examined by Mr. Tieger, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were born and raised in the municipality of Vlasenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what is your educational background, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I completed secondary school. I trained as an engineer after having completed secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from 1975 through 1976, you completed your compulsory service in the Yugoslav national army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let me draw your attention to the multi-party elections of 1990. And let me ask you first, however, to indicate to the Court the ethnic demographic breakdown in Vlasenica in 1990.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: There were 34.817 inhabitants in the municipality of Vlasenica according to the 1991 census. 55.3 per cent were Muslims, 42.5 per cent were Serbs, and 1 per cent were Yugoslavs, 1.1 per cent were the others. And there were 0.01 per cent of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the principal parties contending for electoral posts in Vlasenica in 1990 were the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the results demonstrate that the two key parties at the elections in the 1990s were the Party of Democratic Action and the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the results of the election were 27 members elected to parliament for the SDS, 26 for the SDA, and 7 for the united opposition?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Those were the results after the elections in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a result of the fact that the SDS won one additional seat compared to the SDA, did the SDS then have the right to make the first selection for positions in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No. The party that had the highest percentage of votes had the right to select one of the most important positions in the municipality of Vlasenica. That was the current practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And responding to that opportunity, what position within Vlasenica did the SDS select?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the SDS representatives selected the president of the Assembly, Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic's first name?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Milenko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the SDA then have the right to make the next selection, and did it do so?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the election results, the second-most important position was the president of the Municipal Assembly, and the Party of Democratic Action had the right to select this position. In other words, I was appointed to this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, the translation we received stated that the second-most important position was the president of the Municipal Assembly. I think you indicated earlier that the SDS had already selected the position of president of the Municipal Assembly. Can you clarify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the key position was naturally the head of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and the second key position was the president of the Executive Board. The SDS took the opportunity to appoint Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as I believe you indicated, you assumed the position of president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in a statement that was taken in October 1994, Mr. Redzic, you indicated that the Executive Board or Executive Council was responsible for organising and coordinating all economic, financial, political, and administrative activities in the city, in accordance with the state laws, that it reported to the city parliament. Can you tell us what body at the republic level the Executive Board at the municipal level was comparable to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Executive Board in the municipality was a sort of mini-authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was the government at the level of the municipality. It was a sort of mini-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was your position within the municipality then roughly comparable to the position of the Prime Minister or president of the government at the republic level?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the positions were the same, but the scale was not as large. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina coordinated work at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But my tasks were at the local level, at the level of the Municipal Assembly. I was to do the same sort of things that we were supposed to do on the basis of the law and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, I want to take you next to a period in approximately the middle of 1991, but before I do, I want to ask you very quickly about the nature of relations between the two ethnic groups in Vlasenica as you were growing up and up to approximately the time of the multi-party elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As far as relations between those two groups are concerned, only Muslims and Serbs lived in that territory. There were no problems of a national kind until the break-up of Yugoslavia, or rather, until the conflict in Croatia, which then spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention, then, to the period of mid-1991, around the time of the outbreak of the war in Croatia. Did you become aware of any military activity in the area of Vlasenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time the conflict was raging in Croatia, in Vlasenica paramilitary units had already been formed. They were located in Milici, and they were the strength of a brigade. Between 1.200 and 1.500 troops were in those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did the existence of that brigade come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At the time, the brigade wasn't concealed. It wasn't far from the roads. It was at the end of the playground in Milici by the road itself. These troops maltreated pupils, travellers, they then put up barricades. They wore Chetnik insignia, they wore cockades, and they wore things that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond instilled fear among the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to -- first of all, did you receive complaints or information from citizens at the area of Milici and other parts of Vlasenica concerning this brigade and the activities of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As I have said, the brigade was located in Milici, which is 14 kilometres from Vlasenica. Behind Milici there's a large number of large villages with Muslim inhabitants. Each day pupils had to go to Vlasenica. The villagers had to go to work in the municipality and elsewhere, and these are problems that they had to confront. And they would come to see me to talk about these problems, or they would come to see other people if I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how did you attempt to respond to the complaints of the citizens who came to you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I tried, together with my colleagues and people from the authorities who belonged to the Serbian people who were representatives of the SDS, to talk to them, and we decided that such things were not needed in our areas because they could only result in more trouble and damages. But I must say that in conversation, they just put lip-service to our decisions, and the situation in the field was absolutely the same. Nothing changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there regular military units or troops in the area of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The regular army was in Han Pijesak, 18 kilometres away from Vlasenica. There was nothing in Vlasenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Han Pijesak is an adjacent municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak is 18 kilometres from Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you make an attempt to contact the regular military -- or authorities from the regular military in an effort to address --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to leading in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be more than happy to try it this way, in that case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, in the statement taken from you in October 1994, you indicated in paragraph 17 that you had several meetings with the commander of the regular military forces in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to approaching it from that angle as well. Again, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out -- you objected against the question. Let me first ask the witness. Could you please take your headphones off for a second, but first answer the question: Do you understand or speak any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please take your headphones off for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber finds that the very last part of your question was leading to the extent where you said: "In an effort to." So you may ask the witness about whether he attempted to contact the regular military or authorities and then ask him why he did so. Yes, please proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did you make an attempt to contact the regular military authorities in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, I held meetings at my initiative with the chief commander of the army and commander of the barracks in Han Pijesak, Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were you hoping to achieve by meeting with the commander, Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to avoid confusion in Vlasenica. I've already said that the paramilitary units were located in Milici. What I wanted from Commander Milosevic was to ask for something that is provided for by the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If there was something going on in Vlasenica, we could mobilise the Territorial Defence, which was under the authority of the civilians, and this Territorial Defence would have on its strength both Muslims and Serbs who could protect the population in case of incidents. These units could have protected all the citizens, regardless of their faith or ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify: Who had the authority or constitutional power to mobilise the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: According to the law and constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence and civilian protection are under the authority of the civilian authorities, and it could be mobilised in case of natural disasters or other circumstances, storms, large-scale fires, and also in case of war, they could they could be mobilised by the civilian authorities in order to protect everybody across the board and provide services in case of such large-scale natural disasters. And let me just add to that. In case of a war, these units are subordinated to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, why you went to Commander Milosevic in connection with the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The reason why I saw Mr. Milosevic was not the fact that I was prevented from doing that by the constitution, but the fact that in 1988 and 1989, the JNA had taken all the weapons and all the other materiel and equipment that is regulated by the law as something that the Territorial Defence and civilian protection should have. For that reason, the army had known already a couple of years before that what would happen, and they had removed all the weapons that didn't belong to the JNA but to the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I ask the next question, let me ask you if you know Commander Milosevic's rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: He was a colonel, and his deputy, Asim Dzambasovic was also a colonel. And later on, Mr. Milosevic was the commander of Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So you went to see Colonel Milosevic in order to seek the weapons that had been taken from the TO previously in order to make its mobilisation meaningful; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would object to Mr. Tieger putting words into the witness's mouth. I think it's preferable if Mr. Tieger asks the purpose of the meeting as an open question, as opposed to positing the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, what did Colonel Milosevic say to you when you sought the weapons that had been removed from the TO previously in order to mobilise the TO?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify: I didn't ask for the weapons from the colonel. I asked for the Territorial Defence to be mobilised in the way it had been organised, and I wanted Mr. Milosevic to have control over the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence to protect all the citizens of Vlasenica municipality. In my conversation with Colonel Milosevic - not only in one, in many of them - I introduced as many people from the Muslim and Serb ranks who belonged to other parties. And the answer was always that a Muslim cannot be given a rifle, because that rifle would be turned against the Serbs, and the Serbs would be shot at from that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you tell Colonel Milosevic about the kinds of activities by the paramilitary brigade that had been reported to you by the citizens in the area?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was already abreast of that. He was aware of the paramilitary units, and he even said that this was necessary, that the Serbs should have the military that would protect them. And even despite the existence of the JNA, he thought that there should also be paramilitaries, and these paramilitaries would later on be responsible for all the rapes and killings and murders and whatever had happened in Bosnia afterwards and that you're all familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify that question: Did you relate to Colonel Milosevic the complaints of the local Muslim citizens about the treatment they were receiving from a paramilitary brigade?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. That was the very reason why I went to talk to him. I wanted to hear from him what the officers of the JNA thought of that, and we also wanted to ask them to exert their influence on those paramilitaries. At that time, there was already a difference between the regular units of the JNA and the others. Mr. Milosevic made rounds of the paramilitaries in Milici and in other localities. It was not just the case in Vlasenica and in Milici. So most probably, the role and the task of his as an educated officer was to form these paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just in relation to the last couple of questions. I think it might be appropriate at this point to direct the witness to actually answer the question that's asked by the Prosecution. The last question was asked twice, and in the response a number of other areas that of course basically went into speculation and probabilities and what have you that weren't in fact directly related to the question asked by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If a witness answers a question and deals with matters which are not exclusively within the framework of the question, it's up to the party examining the witness to see whether it's relevant for its case. It might cover a matter that would have been asked anyhow at a later stage. Of course, if it leads to speculation and to assumptions without a clear basis, then the examining party is under an obligation to clarify what that unexplained statements are based upon in terms of facts. But if a witness seeks a path which is not entirely what was in the question, then it's really up for the party examining the witness to see whether it's of any use to let the witness continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but I just want to make a marker at this point, because it's quite clear from, in particular, the last two questions that the matters that are gone into are matters going beyond a response to the question and into matters of speculation, and I want to put that marker there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did other military leaders or figures visit or make rounds of the paramilitary brigade in Milici?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The units located in Milici were visited by the statesmen, such as General Gracanin, who was at the time minister of the interior of Yugoslavia. And then the leading people from the SDS who were down there, unfortunately, during that visit, there was also Mr. Delimustafic, minister of the interior. So there were Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Koljevic, and all the others, all the other key figures of the SDS and people who occupied the highest positions in the BiH government at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was this a publicised visit?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was broadcast on Bosnian television, on Television Belgrade. It was no secret that there was such a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned General Gracanin who was at the time minister of the interior of Yugoslavia. Were there other high-ranking JNA figures who visited the brigade in Milici?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: General Djurdjevac, General Kukanjac were regular visitors, and there were probably the planners of all that. They were formerly officers, and as far as these military structures are concerned, they were the leaders, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, do you know whether, in addition to the formation of this paramilitary brigade, whether or not others in Vlasenica were being armed or receiving arms during this time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I've mentioned the formation of this brigade in Milici. Much before that, there were smaller units in the villages. They were a bit further away from the roads and from the eyes of the people. But let me just give you this by way of example. In spring 1991, there was a ban on felling for the companies in Vlasenica, because there was already the military there, together with their weapons and equipment, and they did their training there. So even before the brigade in Milici was established, there were smaller units which were located in various villages across forests, and they were far away from the eyes of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to these either smaller units or the brigade that was formed in Milici, did you learn whether or not other -- did you learn whether or not Serb civilians were being armed during this period?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object again. The Prosecutor has asked the question in relation to arming. It was not answered in the way that Mr. Tieger liked, and now it's being sought to be led, and I object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two issues. First, ethnicity, and second, civilian against military units. Let me ask you the following, Mr. Witness: You told us about paramilitary units, the one you specifically mentioned, smaller ones. Were weapons available only in those military units, or paramilitary units, or would other people have weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, the Serbian people were fully armed. I was talking about one bigger and many smaller units. Generally speaking, the Serbs were fully armed. When I made rounds of the villages, of the Serbian villages, together with President Stanic, I would see uniformed people with cockades and automatic rifles that had been given to them by the JNA, also the police. I as the president of the Executive Board received Serbs from the faraway villages. They knew who I was. They addressed me as Mr. Stanic. And they said the Serbs -- the Serbs are giving weapons to the SDS and not to us. My answer was: Once the SDS is provided with weapons, it is your turn next. I did not even tell them I was not Mr. Stanic. I hid that fact because there were things already boiling. I wanted to find out some things, and who better to find things from but from peasants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your answer, do you refer to Serbian civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Serbian civilians were also armed. Everybody was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, in the answer we received in English, it says, in part: "They knew who I was. They addressed me as Mr. Stanic." Can you clarify that, please. Did the people from the villages who came to see you know who you were and how it came about that they addressed you as Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Those people came from the faraway villages. They never saw me before. They didn't know who I was. They never saw Stanic either. My secretary shared her office with Mr. Stanic's secretary. Whenever Mr. Stanic was absent, the parties came to see me. And that's why they came to me, believing that I was Mr. Stanic. It didn't happen just on one occasion; it happened quite a lot of times that Mr. Stanic was absent, people would be sent to me, and they were under the false impression that I was Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You stated that the Serbs from these faraway villages told you [Microphone not activated] that the Serbs are giving weapons to the SDS and not to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you stated that the Serbs from those faraway villages told you that the Serbs are giving weapons to the SDS and not to us. Did they tell you who was distributing those weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that Rade Bjelanovic, the chief of MUP, gave weapons to the members of the SDS and not to them. My answer to them would be: When all this is over and when they are all armed, then your turn will come, so don't panic. You will get your weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Rade Bjelanovic a member of SDS?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the leaders of the SDS, and it was the SDS that delegated him as the chief of the Vlasenica MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you may have indicated this earlier, but why did you tell the Serbs who came to see you that when all that was over, then their turn will come, so don't panic, they will get their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to get as much information from the field, from those faraway villages. Had I said anything, the flow of information would have stopped. If Stanic was not there, my secretary would channel all these people to me. And had I revealed my identity to them, then all this information would have stopped. And the best source of information were these people from the faraway villages, who didn't know either Stanic or me. That's why I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did these people from the faraway villages indicate to you whether anyone other than Rade Bjelanovic or any other group was involved in the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It is only logical that the SDS played a key role in the arming of the Serbian people. Rade Bjelanovic most probably distributed the reserve weapons that the MUP had in their depots. Whether he received any weapons from the JNA, I wouldn't know. But I know that a lot of the weapons in the MUP consisted of Zoljas, mortars, automatic rifles, rifles, and explosive devices. So even if he had distributed only that and nothing else, we would still be talking about huge quantities of ammo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Serbs from these faraway villages who came to see you explain to you why they wanted weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, even when I went to other places with Mr. Stanic, their motto was they would say that the Turks wanted to kill them, how they wanted a Jihad state, et cetera. The inhabitants were frightened. They were terrified. And even those who weren't in favour of weapons had to accept such SDS requests, such behaviour, because of these constant lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was it that the villagers -- the Serb villagers from these -- who came to see you were afraid of? Who did they fear wanted to -- who did they understand wanted to kill them?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably had been told that the Muslims wanted to kill them. I spoke to them, asked them whether they lived with Muslim neighbours and they said yes. I asked them whether they had ever had a conflict and they said no. I asked them why they were so afraid now, and they said their leaders had told them that something of the sort would happen. They said that they had no other solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you yourself hear information through the media or any other source indicating that the -- that Serb officials were advising people that the -- that they were in danger from Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic's address in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of the key conditions. This was indirectly an address in which he said that a people would disappear. And he was of the belief that the Serbs should take up arms, in fact, and get rid of all those who were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention for a moment, Mr. Redzic, to the MUP and to the police force in Vlasenica. First of all, was that comprised of both active professionals and a reserve force?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: There were professionals in the police force up until the time when the conflict in Croatia broke out. Since the situation was becoming increasingly complex, there were incidents, problems throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the reservists in particular were sent to Okucani, Slavonija, Osijek, Vukovar, so this was one of the preconditions, the fact -- for the fact that the Presidency and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided that the reserve police force should be mobilised in addition to the active police force. They were to take action in the field and protect citizens and their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a point at which the republic government took steps to -- concerning the composition of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency and the government took decisions, since the MUP was, in organisational terms, part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all orders came from above. They were then directed to the municipal level, to police chiefs. They requested that the reserve force should be balanced, or rather, that both parties should be equally represented, both groups should be equally represented. They didn't want the professional force of one ethnic group to be dismissed in favour of another ethnic group. So the reservists were a problem. It was necessary for the number of reservists to correspond to the number of inhabitants. The chief of police never respected this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there ever any instruction or directive, to your knowledge, to change the -- from the republic government, to change the ethnic composition of the active or professional force?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was forwarded through the government and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They informed the president of the Assembly and the president of the Executive Committee. And through the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the chief of the MUP in the Vlasenica municipality was informed. I personally tried to implement that order, and I spoke to the chief of the MUP, Mr. Rade Bjelanovic. But he never wanted to respect this order, and it's not difficult to figure out why, because we know that the units they had did not suit them. We know that the units that consisted of both Serbs and Muslims did not suit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify: What was the order that you personally tried to implemented and went and spoke to Mr. Bjelanovic about? What did it request?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, this order came from Sarajevo. It requested that reserve police force should be mobilised but on a basis of parity. 50 per cent should be Muslims and 50 per cent should be Serbs. And since I was to be informed about this, as well as Mr. Stanic, I tried to implement this order. Since the situation was becoming increasingly complex, it would be best if there were both Serbs and Muslims in the police force or in the army. This was what I supported. But Mr. Bjelanovic never respected this order. He was never in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in between. You repeatedly told us that Mr. Bjelanovic did not respect the order. In what way? Were there more Muslims, more -- there were no Croats, as far as I understand. Were there more Serbs in the police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the reserve police force consisted of about 170 members. There were 30 or 40 Muslims in that force. That's as far as the reserve force is concerned. As far as the active force is concerned, there were 34 policemen, 6 of whom were Muslims. And we didn't request that Muslims should be brought after having dismissed Serbs, because we knew what that would have led to. At least this is something that I tried to avoid in the territory of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you indicated that you knew that the units that consisted of both Serbs and Muslims did not suit Mr. Bjelanovic. What did you mean by that? In what way did those units not suit him?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The units in which there were Serbs and Croats wouldn't have implemented SDS policies. That is why they avoided forming units that consisted of Serbs and Muslims. We know for what reasons. I don't know if it is necessary to provide further clarifications. Many others have probably spoken about this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you also indicated that you didn't request that Muslims should be brought after having dismissed Serbs because "we know what that would be led to." What did you fear that would lead to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, constant -- the constant threats, the encirclement, paramilitary formations, action taken on all sides. There were problems that arose at the time. And to insist at such a time that Serbs be dismissed from the police force and that Muslims be brought in would have been an excellent motive or an excellent pretext for the Serbs -- or not for the Serbs, but rather for the SDA [as interpreted] representatives to take advantage of that issue and to go into action, according to their plan and according to everything that was subsequently done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek clarification. It appears in our transcript, Mr. Redzic, that you said the following: "To insist at such a time that Serbs be dismissed from the police force and that Muslims be brought in would have been an excellent motive or an excellent pretext for the Serbs, or not for the Serbs, but rather for the SDA representatives --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS. SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did the attempt to -- or did the order to balance the reserve force involve the dismissal of any Serb members of the active force?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The reserve force is an issue. The active force isn't in question. We're talking about the reserve force. These are people who are assigned positions after they have served in the military. They aren't given any sort of compensation. They aren't given a salary or they Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond aren't provided with any expenses. So this wouldn't have been a threat to any of the Serbs who had already been in the reserve force, but only for security reasons. The only reason was to have security for both ethnic groups living in the territory of the municipality of Vlasenica. It wasn't a matter of salaries, of expenses, of per diems, nothing of this sort for the reserve force. The active police had nothing to do with this, and dismissing people was not the issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the issue of dismissing people in that case. During the period of late 1991 through mid-1992, were you aware of any dismissals from employment that took place in Vlasenica on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of 1991, the Serbian directors of companies had already started dismissing Muslims. And on the 15th, or rather, on the 14th of May, there was no one working in an institution of any kind, in companies or state institutions or health institutions. No one who was a Muslim worked in such organisations. So as of the 14th of May, 1991, there wasn't a single Muslim working in any sort of company or institution in the territory of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to seek a clarification, if I may. In your answer, as it appears in our transcript, it says: "So as of the 14th of May, 1991, there wasn't a single Muslim working in any sort of company or institution in the territory of Vlasenica." Is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's when Boksit, which was a key player in economy, which had over 3.800 employees, on the 14th of May, they said that not a single Muslim should return to work. And if by any chance there were any Muslims still working, these were people who were burying the dead, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one additional question, Mr. Redzic. Your previous answer said that: "Towards the end of 1991, Serbian directors of companies had already started dismissing Muslims." And then you continued that: "On the 14th of May," and you later specified the 14th of May, 1991, "there wasn't a single Muslim working in any sort of company or institution." How could the Serbian directors start to dismiss Muslims in late 1991 if they already all had gone by the 14th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was an error. By May 1992, no Muslims were working in the territory of the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let me return momentarily and briefly to the visits you had from Serbs from faraway villages who complained about not receiving arms. Did you bring that information to the attention of any SDS official? Did you complain about it to anyone from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally spoke to Mr. Stanic. I spoke to him and I told him about everything that was taking place in those faraway villages. Because what was happening in the nearby was quite clear. It wasn't concealed. All the inhabitants could see this. But as far as these faraway places are concerned, I spoke to Mr. Stanic about what was happening. He was surprised and asked me where I obtained this information from. He said: "You have better information than I do, I as a member, leader of the SDS." We then went to visit these areas, both the Muslim and Serbian villages, and Mr. Stanic had the opportunity, together with me, to see people who had been lined up in companies, who were in uniform. They were wearing cockades, and naturally, they had automatic weapons on them. We also went to places where there were children between 12 and 15 years of age. We would meet them on the road. We would get out of the vehicle, and we asked those children what they were doing with these weapons. And the answer was that the Muslims wanted to kill them and that they had to be armed to the teeth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I would like to give the opportunity, as requested, to Mr. Krajisnik to address the Court. If this would be a suitable moment for you to have not immediately the break, but to stop this part of the examination and continue after the break. If not, please find a moment soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Redzic, we'll have a break, but apart from that, we have to deal with a procedural issue as well in closed session. So, therefore, we'd like to see you back in -- depends a bit on how much time it will take, but I think it will be a quarter past 4.00. Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Redzic out of the courtroom. Ms. Loukas, would private session do on the issue Mr. Krajisnik would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Private session would be quite adequate. It's just that I understand that part of the matters of Mr. Krajisnik would wish to go into include financial matters, and of course financial matters are of course all subject to confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me turn into private session, and the public is already informed that once we have dealt with this issue, we have a break and we'll resume at approximately a quarter past 4.00. We are not yet in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you escort the witness, Mr. Redzic, into the courtroom. We're in open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, before the recess, you spoke about events in Vlasenica and some of the mounting tensions in 1991 and early 1992. Let me turn your attention, if I may, to the beginning of April 1992. And can you give us some understanding of the state of tension or conflict in Vlasenica at that point, shortly before Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent republic.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The situation in Vlasenica, like in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was coloured by a lot of armed forces, armoured vehicles which were driving constantly from Milici, Sekovici, to Han Pijesak. And this all gave concern to the Muslim population. Tanks were displaying force. People from the SDS and the leaders of the SDS who were not members of the government constantly threatened and caused incidents. The situation was very bad, and every normal person could see that with all the weapons and artillery which could be seen in Vlasenica, all the armed people carrying arms, shooting during the day and during the night in the town and in other places was nothing else but a prelude to the moment when the worst things would happen, such as killings, rapes, looting, expulsion, and other things that happened later on. The Serbian Democratic Party and the key figures in state institutions, after all the provocations against the Muslim population, started and embarked on a final showdown, and they started forcing Bosniaks to agree to the division of Vlasenica into three parts: The Serbian Vlasenica, the Muslim Vlasenica, and Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any local SDS official ever tell you or say in your presence what would happen or what was planned if Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as sovereign and independent?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic and myself participated in meetings with observers every week. On one occasion, a gentleman from the monitoring mission addressed me personally and said to me: "Mr. Redzic, why do you bear with all this humiliation? People are being ill-treated, barricades are being put up, there is shooting going on. Why do you keep quiet?" My answer to him was as follows: "The Muslim people, the Bosniak people, will never wage any wars for any ideals, be it Serbian or Bosniak ideals, or any other ideals." I told him that we were a patient people who would do no harm to anybody. The same gentleman spoke to Mr. Stanic and told him: "Mr. Stanic, your people have arms and force. Why do you not respond to the provocations with your weapons?" He said, Mr. Stanic said: "The moment Bosnia is proclaimed a sovereign state, we will draw up our borders in blood." Unfortunately, this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanic ever tell you or say in your presence where those borders would be and what territory it was anticipated that the Muslims would have?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course, one has to be realistic. Stanic and myself held various conversations and talks, and I asked him to explain things to me, and I asked him: "Even if there was an armed conflict, why should people fare badly?" He told me: "Muslims will be given Tuzla and Zenica, these two enclaves." He told me personally: "Don't go to Sarajevo. There will be a blood battle there." Then I asked him: "Stanic, you have a force at your disposal at the moment. What if the international community turned against you to protect the Muslim people and other innocent people?" He told me: "The international community is lying all the time, and they are saying an entirely different thing to the Serbian people and their leaders."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you mentioned earlier the demand to divide the municipality. I'd like to ask you now to briefly look at Exhibit -- or attachment to, in the potential exhibit list, the attachment to the statement, the protocol for division of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would ask that that be marked for identification and given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P258.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, do you recognise that document and can you tell us what it is, please, if you do.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I absolutely recognise this document. I happened to bring it with me in my pocket. The same document at the time when we feared for our lives. I didn't hand it in to my secretary for filing. It had remained in my pocket. So this is the last straw, aimed at provoking the Bosniak people to justify the use of force. And this is something that the Bosniaks condemned and proclaimed the cause of all their problems. At the beginning we agreed that there would be seven members, that there would be a team on behalf of the Serbs. There would be seven members, and seven members would be representing the Bosniaks. However, one of the people who were proposed on behalf of the Muslims left the area of Vlasenica, and that's why I asked for one representative of the Serbian team to be excluded. And that's how we ended with six representatives of the Serbs, six representatives of the Muslims, or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who presented this document to you, Mr. Redzic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The negotiators from the ranks of the Serbian people drafted this document and handed a copy to everybody present. And this copy, as I've already told you, I kept in my pocket, by pure chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did the negotiations over the division of Vlasenica go on for?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: From the 30th of March onwards, until the 11th, when it was assigned. Realistically speaking, I did not pay any attention to what would be written, but you can see in this document that members of the SDS and members of the government who were proposed by the SDS marked all the points that would be the division points of Vlasenica into three parts. They had everything prepared in advance. They offered us to put forth our proposal. I refused that. And I told them: "Whatever you draft, I will sign, together with my negotiating team." They had everything prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you said that this was the last straw and that you paid little attention to the details, and further, that whatever was drafted, you would sign. Can you explain to the Court why the details of that -- of the division of Vlasenica were not of interest to you in that way.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: There was nothing left to do. Irrespective of everything, people were leaving Vlasenica. They were forced to do that by force, by the paramilitaries, by the soldiers sporting beards, by shooting. Our role, that is, my role, was to just prolong the negotiations in order to enable as many Muslim people to leave Vlasenica during that time. I just didn't want to carry the responsibility for the Muslim victims. I knew that people did not have arms. I knew that Muslims had never been warriors, that they never wanted to oppress anybody. The key thing here is that there was nothing left for us to do in Vlasenica. Every morning -- every minute it could be expected for the units to start moving in from Han Pijesak, Milici, Sekovici and start killing the bare-handed people. My main role was to prolong for as much as I could the negotiations while people were being evacuated towards Kladanj and all the areas where there was a majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you continue, I'm just checking with the third copy we have on our desk. All Judges have been provided with this document. It ends in the original on page 6. At the bottom of page 6, we are in paragraph 5, which reads in English: "As agreed, the municipalities will create conditions," et cetera. But what follows in 6, 7, 8, and as far as signatures and names are concerned, the original is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour. As a matter of temporary expediency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same is true in the copy you just gave to the registrar. So that doesn't help us out. None of the five copies I've seen by now in the original has the last -- well, pages, I take it, 7 and/or 8. Let's continue at this moment, but could you please take care that during the next break we will be provided with the full copy of the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And if the Court wishes, I have a copy here with page 7. I'd be more than pleased to hand it up momentarily so the Court can at least see the significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any question relating to these pages, I would like to receive it now. Otherwise, it will be sufficient to receive it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let me ask you if we can break down into some Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond components some of the events surrounding the demand for the division of Vlasenica. First of all, was this an initiative by the SDS or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It was an SDS initiative, of course. It's as clear as a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you and the other members of the negotiating team on the Muslim side regard it as an effort to end the conflict or end the tensions and as something that could render the Muslims safe if it was agreed to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It never occurred to us to believe that this would be a solution to the problem. It was an SDS initiative, an initiative of the Serbian people to carry out the last provocation. Because they wanted to divide something that was impossible to divide. How does one divide streets, schools, telephone lines, water pipes? How does one divide things that belong to one urban unit? It's just -- it was just out of the question. If you look at this division and if you look at the boundaries of the newly established municipalities that they had in their heads and that they drafted on somebody else's instructions, you will see that Muslims who would have remained in Vlasenica would need a passport to get from one part to another part of Vlasenica. Because this division would have cut off parts of the town. So this was just stupid, not only for us Muslims, but also for the Serbs. Even people in the negotiating team realised that, but I'm sure that they had their orders from a different level as to what they were supposed to do. So the last thing to do was to complicate things beyond belief in order to draw Bosniaks out of the area. I was somebody who wouldn't allow for any Muslim to react to any events. It was their duty to come to me and leave it to me to try and solve it in a peaceful way, because I knew what lay ahead of these people after all that I had seen in the streets, in the town, in the villages. All that instilled fear amongst people was there. You know, everybody knew what tanks were there for, what automatic rifles are there for. Those were not people who were on their way to go hunting. Those people were determined to destroy everything that was not Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any SDS representative tell you what would happen if the Muslims did not agree to the division that was proposed?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The most impertinent [as interpreted] person -- there were other Serbs who were wiser and who did not threaten publicly, so the most impertinent person was Mr. Tomislav Savkic, who personally told me and the rest of the negotiating team if we wanted to bypass this negotiation or stall, there are tanks ready to shed blood and to start moving on from Han Pijesak and Milici. My role there was to just prolong this division, not because I had to do that, but I knew that this was their weak point. My stress was always put on the Boksit mine, which is the largest in Europe and the backbone of the Vlasenica economy. I told them: "If we're going to divide the municipality, then you have to bear in mind that this is the area where Muslims lived."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, may I direct you to listen carefully to the questions and to focus your answer on what has specifically been asked. The last question was whether any SDS representative told you what would happen if the Muslims did not agree, et cetera. So, because we are under some time restraint, and I also do understand that it raises quite a lot of memories in your mind, but what Mr. Tieger wanted to know is who said what would happen. And if he's interested in further consequences, he'll certainly ask you about it. So may I ask you to really focus on the question asked to you. Yes? Thank you in advance. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you mentioned Mr. Savkic. What was his position with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomislav Savkic was the president of the SDS of Vlasenica municipality, and he was the one who uttered the words that the borders would be drawn up in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Savkic's position on some of the other issues in Vlasenica that you have spoken of? For example, the paramilitary formations or the increasing tensions in the area.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As ever, his position was that this was a regular force, that the Serbs had the right to have their army, and that in addition to the JNA, they had the right to arm some other units. It was very difficult to talk to him. There were some other Serbs who were more tolerant, and one could speak to them, but not to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Savkic give speeches intended to encourage other Serbs toward his views?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this on the basis of leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any response to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose it is possible to go through a series of questions leading up to that information, but I hardly think in this context that this is an improperly leading question. It certainly is one that the witness can answer yes or no without being led to one answer or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may answer the question, Witness. So the question was whether Mr. Savkic gave speeches which intended to encourage other Serbs towards his views.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you give us some idea of the nature of those speeches.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: He spoke about Serbs being threatened, that Serbs would be killed, eliminated from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Muslim Jamahirija would be formed and so on and so forth. He would say everything that would instill fear amongst people. They used words to poison the Serbian people, and I still believe that most of the Serbian population was against the war. However, they used methods to poison their minds. They lied to their people. They told them that there is a threat of their disappearance from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, was any SDS republic-level leader or prominent figure present during the course of these negotiations over the division of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In my office where the negotiations took place, there was nobody. However, in the room across the hall, where Mr. Milenko Stanic was, there was a large number of Serbs, intellectuals, members of the industry, COs, and amongst them was Mr. Rajko Dukic. He was in Stanic's office. I repeat: He was not in my office, that is, in the office where the negotiations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Dukic hold with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, he was the president of the Executive Board of the SDS. Later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not any of the materials that were used during the course of the negotiations, the draft documents, any maps of Vlasenica and so on, were held in Mr. Stanic's office?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: All the paperwork, all the professionals who were dealing with the maps, were in Stanic's office. There were some breaks in our negotiations, the negotiations between the Serbs and the Muslims, and as soon as there was a break, the Serbian negotiations would go to Mr. Stanic's office and the Muslims would remain in the room where the negotiations took place, that is, in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The protocol, the document that you have in front of you, makes mention of weapons and turning in weapons. Was there any demand by the SDS for Muslims to turn in weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Members of the SDS asked Muslims to return their weapons. Because of all that happened in the area, I claim in full responsibility that Muslims had nothing but hunting weapons. But we did not even want to look at this document. It was not important. And let me just draw your attention to the fact that by the law and constitution, we were not well prepared to establish municipalities. Municipalities are formed by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is the Assembly that has to establish municipalities after a referendum, because it is required by law that two thirds have to be in favour of the establishment of a new municipality. We, as negotiators, did not have any authority vested in us to form a new municipality whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When the demand for weapons was made, did you tell Mr. Stanic or the other SDS representatives that Muslims had nothing but hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was even a little provocative. All you can write down here is that the Muslims should return their souls to you. How can they return something that they don't have? All they had were hunting weapons. It wouldn't be a problem to go public and to ask people to return these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Stanic or the other SDS representatives say anything to you that indicated whether they believed that the Serbs -- that the Muslims had something more than hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably thought that the Muslims had some sort of weapons, but apart from hunting weapons, people had nothing. They weren't in favour of war. There weren't any weapons to be distributed in Vlasenica. I don't know what would have happened if anyone had offered us weapons, offered them weapons. I wouldn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you advise officials outside Vlasenica about the ongoing negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course. I spoke to the late Alija Izetbegovic, because I knew I was doing something that was against the constitution and against the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I wanted to confer with him so as to avoid suffering the consequences in the future. Perhaps a peaceful solution could be found. In such a case, I would have accepted the responsibility to do something that I wasn't competent for. Mr. Izetbegovic said: "Stall for as long as possible to get the people out." Because the people weren't organised. They didn't have weapons or anything else. They didn't have any possibility of surviving in that territory, given what had happened or was happening to the Muslim and Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how did you and other Muslim officials hope that this crisis would ultimately be resolved? Was there hope that the international community would take steps?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, when these paramilitary institutions were formed by Republika Srpska, we were all participants in that affair. I personally spoke to Mr. Izetbegovic again and I said that it was dangerous, that the situation seemed hopeless for the people. He insisted that we shouldn't panic and said that there shouldn't be any problems caused by Muslims. He said that everything that the Serbian Democratic Party was doing amounted to forming para-institutions, and it's true to say that there was a Republika Srpska, there was a Serbian Assembly, Serbian Autonomous Regions, et cetera, et cetera. Mr. Izetbegovic said that there shouldn't be any problems and that Muslims should not establish a precedent or do something that might serve as a pretext for chaos. And he said that everything that the SDS was doing, he said that the formation of paramilitary institutions, et cetera, he said that the international community would force the Serbs to reverse these acts and to create normal Bosnia which would be the state for all ethnic groups, for the Muslims, for the Bosniaks, for the Croats, and for other people living in its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you indicated earlier that the agreement was in fact signed on April 11th. Did you leave the Vlasenica municipality shortly after that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 18th or the 19th of April that I left Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Stanic after the agreement for division was signed but before you left the municipality, about what was happening in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I phoned Mr. Stanic and said I would come to his flat. He was single at the time, and this is what I did. We sat down, had a cup of coffee and spoke to each other like normal people. I said: "Mr. Stanic, since there's a threat to your people too, from my people, I'd like to tell you what should be done and what is expected." Mr. Stanic on that occasion said: "Redzic, you're in my flat right now, but if they found us here, you'd be killed in the market place, together with me." And this would be for one reason alone -- can I clarify this? I had been accused by a military court of the JNA for having sent back a brigade located in Zaluzani. This was a brigade that was supposed to go to Okucani in Croatia. And indictment was brought against me towards the end of September. It was Article 205, paragraph 1 and 3 of the criminal law of the SFRJ. And from then onwards, it was a question as to whether I would be eliminated or arrested and delivered to the military court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, what did you mean when you said to Mr. Stanic: Since Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond there's a threat to your people too from my people? What threat were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the destruction of anything -- everything that wasn't Serbian. It's not necessary to be very clever. With events in Croatia, in Zvornik, given the fact that the artillery had opened fire, there were Serb units that were engaged from Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, et cetera. Mortar shells were falling. The inhabitants of Vlasenica could see all of this, just like myself. So I couldn't expect any sort of joy or happiness. I wanted him to tell me what he realistically expected, because I believe that if someone should go from Vlasenica, this should be the officials from the SDA and certain other individuals. Stanic told me: "Redzic, we need the villagers. We need the workers. Don't worry about them." Because I told him that he would be held responsible in the future. The war would come to an end, the chaos would come to an end, but someone had to be held accountable for the people who had gone missing. The answer was: The Serbs need the villagers and the workers, the Serb state needs them too. Nothing will happen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the answer is still not entirely clear to me. I don't know whether you are considering the same. But perhaps I could ask you, Mr. Redzic: You said Mr. Stanic -- that you said to -- let me just -- you testified that you said to Mr. Stanic that there was a threat for his people as well. Your last answer seems to indicate, but I do not know whether I correctly understood you, is that the threat to the Serbian people would be that they would be held accountable for what would happen. Is that the threat you had in mind, or was there anything else in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said if the Serbs were threatened by my people, by the Muslims, in such a case, I would be open and frank. And I would say: Mr. Stanic, what sort of fate will I and my people have, or rather, you and your people have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you did not say that there was a threat, but you just suggested what the situation would be if there would be a threat against the Serbian people. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the situation had been inverted, if the Serbian people, together with their leaders, were in the situation that the Muslim people and their leaders were in, say if the situation had been the reverse, if the Serbs were threatened by the Muslim people, in such a case, I would have been frank and I would have said what the fate of that people would be. Because I insisted that the people, if necessary, should be evacuated, and if the villagers were to go, then I would tell the people and they should be evacuated towards Kladanj where the Muslims were. But his answer was that the Serbian republic and the Serbs needed the workers and the villagers, and that that category of the population wouldn't have problems of any kind. But we have seen that it is that category of the population that suffered the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of the negotiations over the division of Vlasenica, did Mr. Stanic or any of the other SDS representatives indicate to you whether it was their idea to divide the municipality or whether the idea had come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the form of this question. The question can be asked in a fashion that does not suggest the possibilities as Mr. Tieger has suggested in his formulation of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You find it not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. So, Witness, you may respond to the question, which was whether Mr. Stanic or any of the other SDS representatives indicated to you whether it was their idea to divide the municipality or whether the idea had come from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Stanic told me that there were no more possibilities, and he said that these orders had come from higher up. He didn't say who they had come from, but I assumed who they had come from, from the SDS head office, and that was an end to the matter. Leaders had issued the order and forwarded the order to local levels, to the SDS and municipal organisations, and they forwarded it to the people who were members of the authorities, people who were also from the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you told us earlier that you left the municipality at some point shortly after the signing of the protocol. Did you stay in contact with people from Vlasenica after you left?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, while the phone lines were still working, I would often speak to Mr. Stanic and some other people, for example, Brano Drakulic. I would speak to them to ask them to provide transport for people who were already moving in the direction of Kladanj. I requested that they help them get to these areas, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what response did you get from Mr. Stanic or Mr. Drakulic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Since we knew each other, they always said there won't be any problems. We'll do whatever we can. They probably wanted to cleanse the area of the non-Serbian population, and many of my requests were implemented. A lot of them -- a lot of the inhabitants were transported in the direction of Kladanj. That was until all the phone lines, all the channels of communication, were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I sense that at this point the witness should be redirected to actually answer the question, as opposed to adding in probabilities and speculations of the nature that were inserted into that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's one point of speculation, that is, what they probably wanted to do. Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the question is rather -- the answer is entirely a matter of facts, and of course, the Chamber is aware that what they had in mind, that unless we find further information --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless we find further information, that, of course, is not something that we could take into consideration, because it has no factual basis whatsoever. But the remaining part is factual.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Redzic, you will have heard the objection by the Defence. You answered to the question, but you included in your answer what the others probably already had in their minds. That is a rather speculative part of the answer, unless you would have specific facts to your knowledge which would support this opinion. But since you are not asked any further questions until now in this respect, I leave it to that. So would you -- if you answer the question, please stick as good as you can to the facts and leave out speculations on what might have been in whoever's mind. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, during this time, did you also, in addition to your contact with Mr. Stanic and Mr. Drakulic by phone, did you also have contact by telephone with Muslims and/or Serbs living in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were very few Muslims remaining in Vlasenica. We had contact while the channels of communication were working. During that period, I spoke to quite a few Muslims and also to some Serbs who lived in the building. We spoke about what was happening in Vlasenica. But the Muslims were afraid to speak. They were afraid of telephone intercepts. So I could only obtain very little information from them.
