And the Serbs were also afraid that the phones might be tapped, and they were afraid of the consequences they might have to suffer in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you give us some idea of the period of time, for how long the telephones remained in service?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was until about the 15th of June, until the first half of June. That's when it was no longer possible to have telephone conversations or other sorts of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to your telephone contact with people in Vlasenica, did you also have contact with people who fled Vlasenica and came to the area in which you were residing?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was my task and duty to deal with that territory, those parts of the Federation. My task had to do with receiving people expelled from the territory of our municipality. We had to provide them with care and accommodation. Every citizen, every Muslim, or rather, a large number of Muslims, gave statements about everything they had seen in Vlasenica. They described all the events. So we had a very good idea of the situation prevailing in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you learn what happened in Vlasenica after you left?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, after leaving Vlasenica, Vlasenica was occupied a few days later, or rather, the forces of the Novi Sad Corps entered Vlasenica between the 21st and 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the people you talked to about the entry of the Novi Sad Corps indicate to you whether they received information about why the corps had arrived?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this. Of course, hearsay is acceptable in this Tribunal, but if we're going to move from second -- from first-hand hearsay to second-hand hearsay, people that spoke to the witness, the information they received from others, I think it should be a bit more clearly defined as to what level of hearsay we're going to at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you could include to the extent possible, the more details on the sources of information. So if --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're asking about the people you talked about, please specify if any specific information comes out of that, but that could be one of the subsequent questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I certainly intended to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did you speak with people who actually spoke with members of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with people who had come from Vlasenica, and they told me that soldiers and officers were very tolerant and treated the Muslim population in Vlasenica very fairly. And they told them - and they were surprised and astounded - when soldiers came to Muslim streets and houses, and they had coffee and ate cakes. They told them that the Serbian Democratic Party had requested the corps [Realtime transcript read in error "court"] to go there because between 300 and 350 Serbs had had their throats cut. When they arrived, these people naturally spoke to Serbs and Muslims, and the Serbs told them that there was no incident of any kind, and no murder had been committed, and 300 to 350 Muslims, as said, didn't have their throats cut. So what's important to point out is that when the Novi Sad Corps was there, they behaved in a very fair way, but before they left, the soldiers said: "When we leave Vlasenica, it will be very difficult for you." They told them that they would leave all the weapons and artillery in Vlasenica and that that is when they could expect a catastrophe. They themselves didn't know what sort of scale of conflict to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, one small point of clarification for the transcript. On page 55, line 7, it indicates: "They told them that the Serbian Democratic Party had requested the court," is what it says in the transcript. Is that -- is it fair to say that what you meant by that was the corps?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The corps. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Redzic, did you further learn from your contacts with refugees who fled the municipality or with people on the telephone what happened to the Muslim community of Vlasenica after that point?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: After the Novi Sad Corps had left, civilians were killed, for example in the village of Pijuci, Durici, Zaklopaca, and in some parts of Vlasenica. There were victims and the killing started. A camp was formed in Vlasenica, the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time whether the same SDS figures who had been in power before you left remained in power in Vlasenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The people who were there before the war broke out continued to hold their positions, and later on they were rewarded and were given positions in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that last question and answer. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Your Honour, I think it's appropriate that it be clarified from whom that information came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course you could have asked this in cross-examination, but I think there's no point in asking the witness, apart from that it's Prosecution time and not Defence time. But apart from that, could you tell us, Mr. Redzic, who exactly told you that the same persons, the same SDS figures who had been in power before you left remained in power in Vlasenica at that time. Could you tell us who told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not difficult. We could receive Serbian television, and we had the opportunity to see who from the SDS was in what position. I'm sure that in Republika Srpska they could receive all of the television of the Federation. So it was the key element that pointed to the fact that all the Serbs from the SDS who were in positions before the war continued to hold either the same positions or higher positions at the levels of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your answer now focuses on the Republika Srpska. The question was about Vlasenica. Did you see -- well, let's say SDS leadership or SDS people in power on television as well, specifically in relation to Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Of course. I saw Stanic, I saw Mr. Savkic. All these people could be seen on Republika Srpska television, together with the positions that they held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what time the Court wishes to break. I received a note indicating this might be the appropriate time, but I leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break of some 20 minutes. But could you give us an indication on how much time you would still need for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would imagine we'll be finished in the first 15 minutes following the break, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes following the break. And may I take it, Ms. Loukas, that the Defence is ready to start cross-examining the witness if we would -- if that would be in some 40 minutes from now?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can indicate just in relation to that, that I can start and go up to a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But there are certain matters that have arisen as a result of the witness's evidence today that require me to -- I will not be in a position to complete my cross-examination today. And I may not, in fact, use up all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll then have a break now for 20 minutes, and once Mr. Tieger has finished, you'll start cross-examination. And then you will continue tomorrow. But let's try to keep it in the usual time limits, and that is, it was scheduled for four hours, you take a bit less, and 60 per cent would then -- the time you do not use -- try to use your time as good as you can, because otherwise the bookkeeping is --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one matter I'd indicate, and it might be appropriate for the witness to the remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could already ask the witness to leave the courtroom, since we'll have a break anyhow. Mr. Redzic, we'd like to see you back in approximately 20 minutes. Could you please follow the usher. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are significant and quite a number of variations in this witness's testimony from his statement, and it means, of course, that I will need the opportunity overnight to go through the transcript. Because there are not one or two. They're a significant number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the Chamber has seen the statement, and it would not be appropriate to discuss at this moment what the inconsistencies are. You said there's a considerable number. May I ask you also to keep in mind how considerable the inconsistencies are, apart from the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the quantity, also look at the quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: One looks at both quantity and quality, and most importantly at quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for 20 minutes, and we'll restart at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mr. Redzic, you mentioned the information that you received about the killings of Muslims and the camp at Susica after you -- after the time that you left Vlasenica. During the course of your discussions with Mr. Stanic or any other SDS official after the time you left Vlasenica, did you ever raise with them the issue of the killings or the camps?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: While the road was open and while I still had an opportunity to talk to Mr. Stanic, Susica did exist, but at that time there was still no killing. It was just a place through which all the inhabitants of Vlasenica had to go, regardless of their age or sex. They had to go through Susica. Some criteria were applied, according to which women and children were transported towards Kladanj and most of the male population remained in the camp, save for some elderly males who were fortunate enough to be transported to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you were referring to your discussions with Mr. Stanic about providing buses so that Muslims could leave Vlasenica, were you referring to transports so that people who were held in Susica could leave Vlasenica, among other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the leading nature of this question. It's quite possible to ask this question without the additional phrase that might go to suggesting what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness testified that he had discussions about providing transport so the people could leave. He testified about the fact that people were held in the camp. The question is merely whether those two things were linked, and I think that's an entirely fair question that doesn't suggest an answer one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is whether the transportation was -- or the transport provided, whether it concerned people kept in detention or not in detention, in Susica camp. That's a question that can be put to the question. So the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you can answer the question, if you understood it or if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll put the question to you. When you talked about transportation provided for people to leave Vlasenica, was that transportation meant for people that were held in detention or people not held in detention, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said a little while ago was that all the inhabitants from the villages, in view of the fact that the town had already been empty, all those from the villages were brought to Susica, to the camp, and according to some of their criteria, the women and the children were transported to Kladanj with some elderly males. And the rest of the males were kept in the camp, and that's where they stayed. Many of them never arrived to the free territory, and their whereabouts are not known to the very day. Nobody knows where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly: I take it that you said that since everyone had to go through Susica camp anyhow, the transportation could only be for those who came from Susica camp, where most of the male persons were kept, apart from the elderly? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Women and children had to arrive in Susica. Susica was the place which was like a filter for the women and children to be released towards Kladanj, together with some elderly males. The rest of the males were kept there, and most of them never arrived in the territory of the Federation. Most of those males who were kept in Susica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it doesn't contradict my understanding of your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During your conversations with Mr. Stanic, did he indicate to you whether that situation, whether the detention of people in Susica and the subsequent transport of Muslims outside of Vlasenica, were his idea?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: If you are referring directly to Susica and the males detained there, Mr. Stanic said: If there was an exchange, the Muslim males would be exchanged for the Serbs who are in Federation. However, this never came through, which means that a large number of people who were in Susica were actually killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And a variation on that question, if I may. Did Mr. Stanic indicate to you whether or not the idea for this exchange was his?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question has actually been asked and answered. Of course, Mr. Tieger didn't get the answer he wanted, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the question was asked but was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was an answer, but the question was not answered. So Mr. Tieger is allowed to put the question again to the witness. And may I direct you, Mr. Redzic, to carefully listen to the question, because the question was whether the situation, whether it was exchange or keeping males or sending women and children elsewhere, together with the elderly, did Mr. Stanic ever tell you whether this was his own idea, to deal with the matter in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stanic always said that things were no longer in his hands and that they simply had to obey orders from higher levels, and everybody knows what higher levels were. So all the orders were handed down from higher levels to the municipal level, and at the municipal level, these orders were carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you've indicated -- referred, rather, on a couple of occasions now to the higher levels of the SDS and of Republika Srpska. Did you know from your discussions with local SDS officials and from your knowledge of the political scene who the leaders of the SDS were?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: One doesn't have to have a lot of knowledge. It's logical when the paramilitaries were established in Republika Srpska, this was formed by the key figures who were leaders of the SDS and who were at the time amongst the highest ranks of the State organs and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The local politics started with the higher authorities, and it was the task of the local politics to carry out orders. If they refused, they were either removed from the political life or replaced, like anywhere else in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who did you understand --

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Which means that orders came down from certain levels, and those levels were composed of certain people: Karadzic, Krajisnik, the late Koljevic, Mrs. Biljana, and a few other people who were there. They were the creators of Republika Srpska, of its constitution, of its laws. I believe that Serbs are very clever people and that they didn't leave anything to chance. They have all the laws, they have their constitution. I have not studied their constitution or their laws, but one should look at the constitution and the laws of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, within that small group of leaders whom you named, were there any among that group who were regarded, as you understood it, based on your knowledge at the time, as the most important and the most powerful?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik had the highest position in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second-ranking person was filtered according to his merits and appointed to the bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And one cannot say that he was on the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond side, that he was an onlooker of the things that were going on at the time and that -- or that they amounted to at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have another item marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I would first like to -- Mr. Tieger, you put to the witness a question on orders that came down from the SDS leadership, and the witness told us a lot, but there is not a lot of factual basis for his answers. And in order to make these answers assist the Chamber, I would invite you to see whether there's any specific knowledge on the orders coming down or whether it's just a general impression based on the position of the leadership persons he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you referred to the top leadership of the SDS and of Republika Srpska, and then you indicated that orders came from the leadership down to the subordinate ranks of the SDS. The Court is asking for whatever information you have beyond any information you may have already provided in the course of your testimony, that indicates, or that causes you to understand that that was the case, that orders were passed down from the top levels of SDS leadership to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, there's subordination everywhere. There's this relation between higher and lower levels. The local leaders shouldn't have taken steps of any kind. They shouldn't have done anything without having received orders from a higher level. Similarly, if I compare the municipality of Vlasenica and my election, a subordinate municipality was not to do anything without consulting with the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Assembly. I'll provide you with an example. For example, if the Dutch started killing the Chinese, who would be held responsible? It would be the Dutch government, not an individual, not the perpetrator of a given crime. It would be the government of the Netherlands that would be held responsible. Similarly, in this system, the leaders in Republika Srpska and people who had been filtered through the SDS, the main people bearing responsibility for the events were there, at the level of the municipality and of local communes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one small point of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: At the beginning of that answer: "Well, there's subordination everywhere." As I understand it from my case manager, Ms. Cmeric, that should be "everywhere in the world."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's how I understood "everywhere" to be. That is, in any place. So I do understand, Mr. Redzic, your answer, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that you say that you concluded from the general hierarchical structure in the government and in organisations, such as the SDS, that it is only possible that that's how the orders came down, without any specific knowledge on specific orders or specific persons giving that orders to the lower levels, but it's on the basis of the general framework that you concluded that this should have been the case. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you would like me to provide you with some sort of a written document or something like that, but that was impossible. Orders were secret, and we know how they were forwarded. They didn't arrive in the municipal organ. It wasn't possible for me, for example, to examine such an order. They were forwarded through secret channels. Because with the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs wouldn't accept this. So the only form of providing arguments and other relevant documents was via the SDS. They could only be forwarded via the SDS and not via a state institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I was seeking is to find out exactly what the basis of your -- the factual basis of your testimony was. So I do not expect you to produce any secret orders if they existed. Of course, the Chamber fully understands that you couldn't. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as indicated earlier, I was about to move on to a document I wanted marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is the intercept authentication chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I have in front of me a chart. I have in front of me also a couple of what seem to be transcripts of telephone conversations, and I have a CD. Would you like to deal with them together or to separate them? First just the chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First the chart, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll not even look at the rest. Yes. Madam Registrar, the chart would then get number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The chart will be Prosecution Exhibit number P259.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if that could be presented to the witness briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, is it correct that you were provided with an opportunity to listen to copies of intercepted telephone conversations and indicate whether or not you recognised any of the voices, participants?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does Prosecution Exhibit number P259 reflect the conversations that you listened to and the voices that you indicated you -- and the names of the persons whose voices you indicated you recognised?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at that exhibit very quickly. The third intercept listed, indicating a conversation between Rajko Dukic and Tihomir Cavkic, I need to ask you whether you know or knew someone named Tihomir Cavkic and recognised his voice, and if not, why that name is listed here.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Tihomir Cavkic. But when he and Rajko Dukic spoke to each other, he introduced himself. But I don't know him personally, and I wouldn't be able to recognise his voice. As to the other conversations, they were clear to me and I could recognise them. Since these are people who always appeared on television, it wasn't difficult for me to recognise them. Some of them I know personally, and I worked with many of them very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And specifically, did you know Mr. Dukic and Mr. Bajagic personally?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who Zvonko Bajagic is and what his position or affiliations were in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Bajagic I don't know what party position he held, but I knew him from the time of Kosovo, when a lot of Serbs gathered, when Milosevic spoke there. Mr. Bajagic Zvonko went from Vlasenica on a horse in Serbian uniform. He went there and he represented the Vojvoda, the leader for the Serbs. Unfortunately, having listened to those conversations, I'd like to say that it's regrettable that a semi-literate person forwards information to Mr. Karadzic, forwards lies, in order to provoke conflict in the area of north-eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Bajagic affiliated with the SDS in the area of Vlasenica in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the Executive Board, in the Assembly of -- he was in the Executive Board of the SDS in the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also ask that the transcripts and the CD be marked as the A and B versions of this particular exhibit and that they eventually be tendered together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The CD of intercepted conversations will be Prosecution Exhibit number P259A, and the transcripts P259B and P259B.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we take all the five transcripts together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one. Mr. Tieger, you provided to us in 259 a transcript of a telephone intercept. Is there any clue about the date of that first transcript? All the others are provided with a date. The first one is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is no clue available at counsel table at the moment, and I would not be able to illuminate that further without inquiring after court. But I would be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to hear from you, because you can understand that relevance is also depending on the exact moment in time. Yes, thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Redzic, you'll now be examined by Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. There's just a brief matter that I should cover in private session prior to my commencement of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it a matter concerning the witness or is it a matter --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So would it be preferable to ask the witness -- does he have to leave the court or can he take his headphones off? Would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy for just the headphones to be taken off, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we turn into private session. And could you please take your earphones off for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, thank you for your patience. You'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, as president of the Executive Board at the time in Vlasenica, you, of course, had an understanding of the politics of the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think that you've given evidence today that on at least two occasions you'd spoken to Mr. Izetbegovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to this question of the division of the municipality that you've spoken of today in your evidence, I just want to ask you some questions going for context in that area. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken about these negotiations proceeding, as I understand it, from late March through the early part of April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The 11th. The signature was on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: 11th of April, yes. So just in relation to the context in which this was occurring, you, of course, are aware of the negotiations that were going on in the international sphere under the auspices of the European Community in relation to the diplomat Mr. Cutilheiro?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in about mid-February, the international conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina met in Sarajevo, and there was some -- negotiations were conducted; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. That was higher-level politics. But let's say that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sure. And of course, these were matters that were covered in newspapers and of course in television coverage, of course? I don't think there was a translation, but I think I heard the word "da"; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And these negotiations, of course, continued through March, and the leaders of the three national parties in Bosnia actually all signed a declaration on the principles of a new constitutional order for Bosnia-Herzegovina. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No. If you are referring to the new organisation -- I don't know what you're referring to. More specifically. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm referring again to the negotiations surrounding the Cutileiro plan. You knew about the Cutileiro plan, of course?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was just a fancy name that they had for it at the time, but I'll stick to Cutileiro plan, okay? Okay. Now, part of that was that Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain within its borders; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As a single state?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And with three constituent units based on the national principle; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the three constituent units, of course, being the Bosniaks, the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely sure. I was not a member of the higher politics. I did follow the events. Those were negotiations. Let's be clear on that. They were negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the idea being that principles were adopted; correct? You'd obviously be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it was agreed in March that a Working Group would be set up to define the territories of the three different communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And some of the principles dealt with in terms of this Cutileiro plan were that these maps of the constituent units would be based on national principles, economic principles, geographical principles, and also on historic, religious, cultural, educational, and transport and communication criteria?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not entirely clear the extent to which this witness is familiar with the terms of the Cutileiro plan, but even if he were reasonably familiar with it, I can't see the point of a quiz on the content of the Cutileiro plan. If he's going to be asked about the plan, then let's have it in front of him. If we're leading to a particular point, then I think it might be more efficient to move past a recitation of all the details of the plan, which frankly, this witness should not be expected to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, would you like to answer, the witness still having his earphones on, or would you rather ask me to invite him to take them off?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's probably preferable if the witness does take his headphones off, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take your headphones off for a second. Thank you. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just in relation to this, I mean, I'm just setting some brief questions here, setting the political context in relation to which we're dealing with a particular municipality and a particular division that occurred within a municipality, and also, this witness's awareness of the negotiations that were going on in the international community and the local community's awareness of what was going on and what had been projected is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just try to understand you. I do understand that you're seeking a parallel. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Seeking a parallel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Parallel between division, geographical or territorial division on the level of negotiations at a higher level and on the local level. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What I'm dealing with is setting the matters in a context, the fact that people throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina were aware of these negotiations that were going on at the international level and within a particular municipality they would have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the relevance of that awareness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that -- and I don't like to forecast where I'm going in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't know that that's entirely appropriate. But, Your Honour, the relevance is that whilst all of this was going on in the international arena, it's quite clear that local communities would undertake certain activities of their own volition, being aware of this broader international context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I understand to be the parallel situation on the different levels. Of course, if you think that it's important to establish, but apart from to what extent the situation at the local level, well, had some resemblance with what happened on another level, of course, it's also important to see what the difference is. For example, I do not remember that any negotiations on the Cutileiro plan, that, as this witness testified for the local level, that anyone ever said that if you don't accept it, the guns will be there tomorrow. That's, of course -- so I do understand what you're seeking. To what extent the parallel would really assist the Chamber is still to be seen. But please proceed now. Ask the witness to put his headphones on again. But let's not spend too much time. And I do agree with Mr. Tieger that we could try to -- I'm not quite sure whether all the details of the Cutileiro plan are really known to the witness and to what extent it's really necessary to go through all this in detail. If you would say what is the -- your general idea of what the Cutileiro plan was about, well, division of territory, that's, I mean, I think would do for the purposes you are seeking this. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think it may be important to point out, and I'm glad we had the opportunity to hear counsel's response, that to some extent, the thrust of the question and the alleged parallel may be based on a faulty premise. We heard a great deal of evidence, some of which came from the Defence, that the Cutileiro negotiations and especially that part that counsel seems to be focusing on, had broken down by the time the negotiations -- before the time the negotiations in Vlasenica began. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have all the details of time in my mind at this moment. But perhaps you could consider this as well, Ms. Loukas, when you continue to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I already have and that does not create the disconnect. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see what it brings us. But perhaps you could try to do it as efficiently as possible. Could you please put your headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, what was your understanding of the broad agreement that had been reached in relation to the Cutileiro plan?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't speak about superficial things, about Vance-Owen or Cutilheiro's plans, because I just saw this on TV and I read about it. If I were to talk about these two, I would have to have the plans before me, read them. Otherwise, I wouldn't venture into commenting upon them. If there is anything in your statement that you want to ask me about, I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzic. Now, I'm asking you what your understanding was, so far as you can remember it now, at the time, in Vlasenica, of what was going on in relation to the Cutileiro plan.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you anything. I just knew the outlines of those, like so many people. I just watched information on TV. I've never seen the plan itself, and it wouldn't be proper for me to discuss things that I don't know the details of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, if you, as you tell us, you knew the outline of the plan, just give us your global understanding of what it was about. No one blames you for not knowing any details. But since you tell us that you have a general idea, please tell us what it was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be honest with you and tell you that I really don't remember at this point in time. This was 14 years ago, 11, 12, 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask it to you in a different way. Was the plan about joining the different parties in one government, or was it about division of power, or was it about division of territory, or was it about stop fighting? What was the plan at all about? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the multi-party election, the government was formed consisting of all the peoples. The Presidency, the government, and all the other institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina and at lower levels. And this was one of the causes. The mini-division of Vlasenica followed the same principle. So we're talking about a dissolution, a break-up of a unity which was Bosnia-Herzegovina and the annexation of the other parts of Serbian territories too, Yugoslavia, and parts of Croatia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was about division, and you also now mention territory. Was it about territorial division, this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence counsel told me that the division should have been territorial, although formally it should have stayed a single state. This defies any reasoning. One part of Bosnia-Herzegovina would go one way, one part of Herzegovina would go another way. So this is what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, you, at the time, had some awareness of this -- the negotiations going on in relation to the Cutileiro plan, based on your watching TV and reading newspapers; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And so did other people in Vlasenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: TV and newspapers, yes. Those were our sources of information. As the president of the Executive Board, I never saw any of these agreements or plans. I don't know whether it makes any sense for me to discuss the details of the negotiations, the results of which I've never read or seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the witness feels a bit uncomfortable on understandable grounds. If you -- the sooner you come to your point, I think the sooner he might feel at ease again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm sure, Your Honour, he feels uncomfortable, and I'm sure I'll make him feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, the situation is this: I'm not interested in cross-examining you about the fine detail of this document. I'm interested about your knowledge at the time and your understanding of what other people's knowledge was at the time in your municipality in Vlasenica. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I understand your question, but I cannot answer about things that I know only superficially. I understand your question, but what am I supposed to tell you in answer to that question? How am I supposed to answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, first of all, it's 7.00, and that's the time where we usually stop. I nevertheless would like to say the following to you: Whenever there's a question to which you would not know Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the answer, just tell us that you don't know. If someone says: Do you know about the Cutileiro plan? And if you know something about it, just say: I know something about it. If the next question would be: Could you give us any idea of how the -- well, let's say the territorial division would take place; if you know, tell us. And if you say, well, I know that was in two parts, but that's all I know, just answer the question to the level of your knowledge. And whenever you have any problems in doing so, just address me and say: I don't know how to answer this question, or how to understand this question. And we'll certainly sort that out in a way that Ms. Loukas gets the answer to the level of what you can tell her and what you can't tell her, you'll not tell her. Is that clear? Then apart from that, I'd like to instruct you that we'd like to see you back tomorrow, but tomorrow morning, at 9.00, and I'm looking to you, Madam Registrar, to know in what courtroom. It will be in this same courtroom. Tomorrow morning, 9.00. And I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and not to speak to anyone about the testimony you will still continue to give tomorrow. Is that clear? We'll then adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
